Messages.Author: Archon
Messages.Body:
Hi, I'm planning to organise my first tournament soon. It will be a
draft for many players don't have a lot of card and I want them to
have equal chances of victory. What I ask for is maybe some tips or
advice.

- how many booster should I use

- Anything you judge useful

- I will use Gehenna booster, is that a good idea?

Thanks

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>- how many booster should I use

9-10, probably. Less, unless you allow people to bring cards, has problems
with people finding enough cards to fill out decks. More has the obvious
problems of expense and additional time. I'd guess that people would
eventually get bored of drafting more and more cards, though when that
threshold is hit isn't at all clear as I don't specifically recall a draft
above 10 and have my doubts about anyone doing one with more than 12.

>- Anything you judge useful

Do you want to use any mechanic to prevent rare drafting? I run into this
problem all the time with locals. The players want protection from rare
drafting even when they have vast collections, a lot of rares aren't worth
much, and rare drafting tends to hurt fielding a better deck. I don't care
that much about a "keep the rare" rule, but it does reduce strategy somewhat
while only protecting people who cracked good rares.

There are some differences in the types of drafts. Usually we Rochester (table
draft) vampires and booster draft library afterwards. There are various fiddly
things you have to make calls on at times. For straight booster, you need to
make sure that people realize they need enough vampires to fill out a crypt.
For drafting separate piles of cards, you run into nonequal amounts.

To avoid problems, you want to make sure there are no packs in error - too few
cards, too many, whatever - and otherwise be prepared for procedural,
logistical, and whatnot potential issues.

Time can be a problem. Drafting isn't quick and some people won't necessarily
be prepared going in. One of the reasons I never understood drafting at
prereleases is having people either not know what the cards do or having them
waste a bunch of time finding out. It's a lot better when your players don't
have to read the cards for the first time, and this can be avoided by having
people look up cards prior to the draft. Not that this is the only way players
can be underprepared, but it's more common than I'd like.

>- I will use Gehenna booster, is that a good idea?

All Gehenna? That doesn't sound like a good idea. SW and CE (and Jyhad/V:TES
and Sabbat) are good to include to some degree just so there are some basic
cards in the pool so that people's decks aren't completely goofy, but it likely
depends upon your players. Whatever they will find fun is a good idea.

It doesn't seem like there's any perfect combination with Gehenna. Gehenna has
cards that reward playing the Sabbat exclusive and independent exclusive
disciplines, and there's problems finding other sets that work well with that
feature.

I agree. If it is a non-snactioned tournament and your players have
problems with the money, you could include cards from starters. But
tell the players, what starters used, because you will have different
disciplines. (Using BH starters for example, there is no FOR).

> > Do you want to use any mechanic to prevent rare drafting? I run into this
> > problem all the time with locals.

The best mechanic is big prizes for the first players. If you win a
half display, you will not draft bad rares. Simple.

> Hum... I understand the problem but if a player draft all the rare,
> his deck will suffer from it, his winning chance will decrease...

My argument.

> Anyway how have you solve this, what do you mean by protecting rare,
> drafting them apart, limiting the number of rare that a player can
> draft?

To complicated IMO.

> > There are some differences in the types of drafts. Usually we Rochester (table
> > draft) vampires and booster draft library afterwards.

We always use pure booster draft. Its the fastest solution, needs the
most skill and gives the most fun. All theoretical problems discussed
(example, a player hasnt drafted 12 Vampires), will not happen in
reality.

> > Time can be a problem. Drafting isn't quick and some people won't necessarily
> > be prepared going in.

You need a clock. First five cards of a booster 45 seconds, after that
30 seconds.

> > >- I will use Gehenna booster, is that a good idea?

You need boosters from a basic set (Jyhad, Sabbat, SW, CE) or some
starters with basic disciplines. Some boosters from strange strange
expansions are always fun. I would say for example 5 SW, 3 BH and 1
Gehenna would be nice.

An additional advice: The first playing round should not be identical
with the drafting pod. So you will have no problem with counter
drafting.

Messages.Author: Matthew T. Morgan
Messages.Body:
On 28 Aug 2004, Archon wrote:

> Hum... I understand the problem but if a player draft all the rare,
> his deck will suffer from it, his winning chance will decrease...
> Anyway how have you solve this, what do you mean by protecting rare,
> drafting them apart, limiting the number of rare that a player can
> draft?

Some draft tournaments allow players to pick two cards from the first
pack. That way, you can take the rare and take something good for your
deck. Or if your rare is Twisting the Knife (as it so often is), you can
take two cards that are good for your deck.

I've done it both ways and while I don't have a strong preference, I did
pass a Shroud of Absence at one of the GenCon drafts and my deck still
sucked and got nothing done. Regret! I could've had a terrible draft
deck and a Shroud of Absence. Instead all I ended up with is a terrible
draft deck.

Matt Morgan

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>Do you really run into Rare Drafting as a problem? I mean, like, people are
>concerened about it? That is weird. I mean you completely articulate why
>people shouldn't care (most rares not worth anything, really; it is often
>counter productive to making a good deck, whatever), and in my experience,
>people tend to not care. How much do people care, do you find, and what do
>you do about it?

I know at least one person who rare drafts, but it's not rare drafting that's
the problem; it's people thinking that rare drafting will happen and/or not
wanting to lose out in some way by giving up rares that is the basis for the
desire for protection. Even locals with lots of cards don't necessarily track
what is rare or how valuable a particular rare is (lack of appraisal skill). I
think it's a fear out of lack of knowledge. If you know something is
particularly valuable, you can rare draft it without needing protection. If
not sufficiently valuable, then you can focus on your deck instead in the
absence of protection. If something is much more valuable to you than the
other drafters, you can end up with it without protection but not with. Etc.
Again, IMO, protection only helps people who crack *good* rares; it actually
dumbs down the process by not rewarding people who focus on putting together a
good deck. If you crack a War Ghoul or whatever, well, rare draft - plenty of
rare drafting goes on in Magic where the rewards for winning tend to be much
higher. (Course, Magic has an easy fix in pick up drafts in that you can draft
playing for the rares as prizes, something I doubt would go over that well with
V:TES.)

The rule we've used at least a couple of times is that, when you open the
packs, the rare is removed and retained. It's not at all complicated or
difficult.

BTW, I don't at all think giving a big top prize is desirable. Someone
selectively rare drafting might still win and anyone who doesn't win still has
the same incentive to rare draft, possibly more.

Not that I think this is the biggest issue in the world. Our greatest problems
involving draft are such things as the lack of desire to spend money on cards
you don't want and the extra time required which rules out certain locations or
start times.

You are exactly correct. So you can hear an alternate opinion,
I feel Curevei's concerns are overstated. Granted, I don't play
that much draft myself but in the time I've played Magic and
Jyhad (since pretty much the beginning of Magic), I haven't run
across many people who are very concerned about rare drafting.
This is a situation where some people REALLY hate it for some
reason and those folks complain a lot. But the majority don't
seem to care that much. I believe most people react like you do.
For me, the choice to draft a prize rare that drops to me is fun.
Sometimes you get kind of interesting choices between the neat rare
and a good card for the tournament and that's fine. It almost never
happens that a choice turns out to be critical in my experience.
(That is, I've never had to choose between an absolute "God" draft
deck card and a prize rare.)

Besides, I've never heard anyone propose a good rule to avoid this.
The only one worth considering is the keep-your-own-rare rule and
even this doesn't address important uncommons you'd like to keep
because they're good constructed cards. Any other mechanism I've
heard people talk about are solutions that are far worse than the
problem.

Fred

While I am in no way concerened with Rare Drafting in draft play, or
whatever, the best solution (assuming one is necessary for whatever reason)
I have seen mentioned is simply "take 2 cards from the pack you open"--you
can then take the rare and another good card for play. Or if the rare is bad
and you don't care, you can take 2 good cards for play. Strikes me as a very
reasonable solution that doesn't actually specifically address the Rare
Draft issue certainly fixes it and gives people who are drafting to make
good decks and don't care about rares extra good options.

Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message <BD58F8BB.19290%pd...@lightlink.com>,
Peter D Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com> mumbled something about:

>Frederick Scott wrote:
>
>> Besides, I've never heard anyone propose a good rule to avoid this.

Honestly, I've never even heard a good reason as to why it's a problem.

Assume you (generic 'you', not you, fred) have a draft consisting of ten
boosters. You paid for ten rares. You open ten packs first; you have
the option to draft those ten rares, presto, you have ten rares.

"Oh! Oh!", but you say. "But if I draft this Up Yours!, then I will not
be able to take the Blood Doll that will help me build a better deck
that I can use to win the tournament!"

Yep, by golly, you must make this decision ALL BY YOURSELF. And someone
else surely may draft the Up Yours! as it is passed around, and since
everyone else ALWAYS drafts their own rares first shot (since they NEVER
open packs with Blood Dolls in them), all the rares will be gone and you
will be SCREWED OUT OF A RARE OMG LOL UNFAIR NOOO!!!111

However, you will have a better chance of winning the tournament, and
last I saw most tournaments had at least one booster pack for first
place, often more, so you will still get a nice shiny matching rare.

Besides, think of it this way; if the person to your left/right ALSO
rare-drafts, then you can have his Blood Doll instead. And if he
doesn't, then you can just take his rare and hey, guess what: you break
even. Everyone else has to make the same decision you do, and someone
who exclusively rare-drafts is going to hurt their own chances of
winning. V:TES is simply not a rare-intensive game -- I can get much
further with 10x Aura of Invincibility, for example, than I can with 10x
Flash Grenade. (I may have the exact rarity wrong, but you get the
idea.)

So if you run into people who are all up in arms about rare-drafting,
just pat them on the head and say "if you're so worried, take it
yourself."

-- Derek

> even this doesn't address important uncommons you'd like to keep
> because they're good constructed cards. Any other mechanism I've
> heard people talk about are solutions that are far worse than the

One mechanism I have played with in draft is the person who opens the
pack keeps *two* cards, then afterward only one card per pack is kept.
This gives each person the opportunity to keep their rare if they
want, or they can pass it along if they don't find it useful for their
deck.

This solution I think tends to minimize the complaining about
rare-drafting, and not significantly affect the power of cards that
people do draft.

Jeff

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:

> Huh? That sounds like...drafting two cards. That's it? Your big
> solution is to draft *two* cards the first time you choose from
> the pack you opened instead of one?

Umm, yeah? I mean, assuming that the Rare Draft issue is a problem (I can't
imagine that it ever would be, but if, like, you have a group of people who
really have it stuck in their craw that they might get screwed out of a rare
in draft that they don't want to play, or whatever), just draft 2 cards out
of the pack you open. If you want the rare and another card, take the rare.
If you want 2 good draft cards, take those and screw the rare.

>
> I'll say one for it: it doesn't require a lot of explanation
> other than, "Why are we bothering with this?" How 'bout we just
> take the rare card out of the pack we open - if we want it, or
> the best play card if we don't - and then we can choose the second
> best card out of our neighbor's pack? That requires even _less_
> explanation.

Sure. Or, you could just ignore the whole thing and take one card out of
each pack. But assuming someone is upset about Rare Drafting, using the
"take 2 cards out of the pack you open" lets people take their rare and then
another good card. If you just make someone take the rare first, people who
are playing to actually win the tournament are going to be pissed 'cause
they open their pack, see a Blood Doll, and are forced to take the Up
Yours!, even though they just want the Blood Doll. If people make an issue
out of it, let them take 2 cards. The "I don't wanna be screwed by rare
drafting!" people don't feel put out, and the "I wanna win the game" people
feel like they aren't hosed by the rare draft fear people.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Reyda wrote:

> i was just thinking that if people come and play a draft, it's to play a
> game. If they are here to draft rares, they'd better spend the fee on buying
> rares at their local stores, i bet that would cost them less than drafting
> random rares (and often have crappy ones).

See, again, yeah, you are correct. But the issue at hand (that started most
of this discussion) was "I've got players who I want to get to play draft,
'cause I have other players who really wanna play draft and I want more
draft players, but some of theplayers I want to get to play draft are afraid
of Rare Drafting, so they are disinclined to play draft. How do I get them
to draft?"

You are correct that Rare Drafting is not necessarily a good idea. And will
likely make you lose. But the point is that there are, somewhere, a group of
people who are afraid of Rare Drafting, and don't want to play Draft 'cause
they don't want to be hosed by their opponents Rare Drafting. If there was a
built in "fix" for Rare Drafting, then these players, presumably, would be
more willing to play Draft, and then everyone wins.

So the options suggested were:

-Make people take the Rare out of the pack they open.

-Let people take 2 cards out of thepack they open.

The first option is the obvious easy solution, but strikes many of us as
less elegant as the second, which doesn't *make* you take the Rare,and if
you don't want the Rare, you can make 2 good picks out of your pack. That
way everyone is happy--the folks who want their Rares get the rare and
another good card, the people who are trying to make a good deck get 2 good
picks out of one pack.

Yes--simply ignoring the whole thing is an option too, but that is the
option that isn't going to get the folks who are not playing Draft 'cause of
Rare Drafting fear to start playing Draft, which was the whole point of this
excercize.

> Plus if they don't take the draft
> seriously they'll have a hard time going to the finals -where they win
> entire boosters, not single rares. I wanted to put that in a creative way
> but it was a failure, i guess...

No, your illustration worked just fine. But it isn't an illustration that is
going to make people who aren't playing Draft out of fear of Rare Drafting
suddenly realize the error of their ways and start playing Draft. I'd guess
that the "pick 2 cards from the pack you open" plan might.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Derek Ray wrote:

> You explain to them that their concerns about rare-drafting are
> unfounded, using all the arguments posted here.

Yeah, see, that isn't necessarily going to work. This clearly is not a
problem that comes from logic or rationality. It is from people who are
being irrational--fear of rare drafting is clearly irrational. This being
said, if there are people who have this irrational fear, and if you want to
get them to play, you come up with a solution that will likely work with the
irrational fear. Logic is not that solution.

>
> If they still don't get it, there's honestly nothing you can do to make
> them get it; they're stubborn and scared and will stay that way forever.
> Just ignore them and run the draft. =/

Or, you could make a small concession that isn't really going to hurt
anyone, and get a few more player to play draft.

> But there's not a built-in "broken" for rare-drafting.

I'm not saying there is. Ever. But if you've got people who think there is,
and logic fails to convince them otherwise, and you want them to play draft,
you come up with a solution.

> Again, just keep repeating the arguments to them. Point out that their
> position really is "I want to know in advance if my opponents will make
> good decks, or if they're gonna rare draft, so I know whether I have to
> make a good deck too, or if *I* have to rare draft", and how this is not
> a Good Plan for them.

Sure. That works just fine on the internet. But in real life, you likely
just piss them off and make them not want to play even more. Especially
considering how draft isn't cheap--you are trying to nicely coerce folks
into playing expensive draft, 'cause presumably, you want more folks playing
draft. You could try logic. Or repeating arguments. I don't think logic is
likely to work. I think repeating arguments is likely to piss people off. A
simple fix like "pick 2 out of the pack you open" might work just fine with
limitied impact on play.

> Junk, as we all pretty much agree. Forcing an Up Yours! on someone
> instead of the Blood Doll penalizes those who DON'T rare-draft, or just
> don't give a damn.

Exactly.

> This is too much of an advantage for people who are NOT rare-drafting,
> and penalizes the people worried about rare-drafting even more.

I'm not so convinced of that. Picking 2 cards out of a pack is, likely, not
any better than picking the best card out of your pack and the second best
card out your neighbors pack. But the psychological advantage it gives
people afraid of rare drafting is likely enough to convince them to actually
play. And maybe have a good time. And maybe begin to understand draft enough
so that logic will work on them eventually.

Berating people into playing VTES, or any game that is supposed to be

it would be great if we set aside a weekend day locally right after
the current sets are open and played some sealed first, then some
draft after, probably with the 2-pick per pack rule. People would just
take their rares since it's just for fun, but most importantly they'd
get experience drafting and these sorts of concerns about

> people afraid of rare drafting is likely enough to convince them to actually
> play. And maybe have a good time. And maybe begin to understand draft enough
> so that logic will work on them eventually.

I'm with Peter on this one. "God" packs do happen, but everyone has
equal access to the same number of fresh packs so it's not likely to
affect the outcome any more than standard drafting one per pack.
Besides, someone drafting a rare and a power uncommon is probably
doing the right thing anyway.

It's kinda like one of those LSJ/design team arguments where events
affect everyone equally: If your strategy (that is, you decide to
draft "good stuff" and not rares) is designed to take advantage of the
event (draft 2 cards from fresh packs), you'll likely perform better.
So everyone, put lots of Masters in your Anthelios decks. ;)

Bottom line is there are lots of draft options. Do what's best for
your group.

Snapcase wrote:

> I still don't get it, after reading most of this thread. If people
> don't want to get "screwed" by other people rare drafting, they can just
> rare draft themselves, no? Problem solved.

See, here is the thing. If you want to do well in the tournament, you don't
rare draft. You "good card" draft (i.e. you draft to make a good deck). If
you are "good card drafting", and the guy next to you is just "rare
drafting", then the guy next to you gets twice as many rares as he paid for.
If there are 4 people at the table, and 3 of them are trying to make a good
deck, and the 4th guy is rare drafting, not caring what his deck looks like,
guy 4 is going to end up with, what, about 32 rares, and everyone else is
going to end up with none.

So you end up rare drafting, 'cause you are afraid of getting screwed out of
your rares ('cause you equate "buying a booster pack" with "buying a rare",
even in s a draft game). Which means that the guy who isn't rare drafting is
making a much better deck than you, and while you aren't get screwed out of
his rares, and he is, he is much more likely to win the game, and if you
can't win the game, why are you drafting in the first place, rather than
just buying boosters?

Again, I'm not saying this is particularly rational. But it is likely the
understanding of at least some players who might like playing draft if they
could avoid feeling screwed by rare drafting.

Thus, the "pick 2 out of the pack you open" plan, which likely makes
everyone feel comfortable about the situation.

Ok. Dude. The whole point of the discussion (well, at least this part) was
"how do I get people who are irrationally afraid of rare drafting to play
draft?"

Saying "then they shouldn't play draft" isn't solving the problem. Even
remotely.

The "pick 2 out of the pack you open" plan likely will convince these people

any negative impact at all on a local draft game with 8 people, 4 of whom
are only willing to play draft if they don't feel they are getting hosed by
rare drafting.

Yes. I'm sure it would. And you could also say "Hey! Israelies!

It strikes me, at least, that the "draft 2 from the pack you open" plan
could likely be the winning over point. Once they are playing, and have
draft experince, and like doing so, *then* maybe logic will work out. Before
hand, you are just going to end up with people, ya know, not wanting to

Oh, not really _that_ bad... I think what's being lost in all
this debate about what's the best rule to convince irrational
people not to fear rare drafting is that fact that there doesn't
seem to be many such people, at least in my experience. Whenever
I hear about people complaining about "rare drafters", it's always
some other unspecified people - that is, never the speaker himself -
who are supposedly complaining. It's like that old "heard it from
the friend of a friend" thing. Who really stands up and says they
care about this? I can't recall ever meeting such a person.

Make no mistake, I think the logic behind the rule Peter is
advocating is exceptionally silly. I don't see how drafting two
cards makes any difference in the question of having to choose
between a rare valuable constructed card and a good draft card.
What if there are exactly *two* good draft cards in the pack
you open? And if you only draft one card (the normal rules), you
have just as much chance to benefit from your neighbor's difficult
decision as you have of losing out when you have to make one. And
if you and your neighbor would make different decisions, you both
win - that's the beauty of drafting.

But Peter says this rule would somehow assauge the irrational
people who fear rare drafting - as opposed to say, a rule that
forces one to take the rare cards from the packs he opens. (At
least this actually addresses the issue directly.) But I'm not
sure how he can claim to know what such a person would prefer.

Fred

See, I'm guessing that the psychological trick of getting to take the rare
*and* another good card would likely convince someone who fills this
description that drafting isn't that scary. But then I'm totally talking out
of my ass here.

> But Peter says this rule would somehow assauge the irrational
> people who fear rare drafting - as opposed to say, a rule that
> forces one to take the rare cards from the packs he opens. (At
> least this actually addresses the issue directly.)

It does, but it also makes the people who are actually wanting to play draft
for draft's sake (i.e. they don't care about the rare) unhappy, as they'll
open a pack, see all the good and powerful cards in their pack, and then be
foreced to pick an Up Yours!. I figure the "pick 2 from the pack you open"
plan will make everyone happy, not negatively impact the game to any
significant extent, and in the end, do exactly what it is meant to--convince
people who are leery of draft to play.

>But I'm not sure how he can claim to know what such a person would prefer.

I can't. But then, I'm apparently the only person involved in this
discussion who accepts that, in real life, berrating folks with logic for
being completely irrational is unlikely to win them over to your side, so
maybe I have a unique insight to the human mind :-)
